newsitem.title: USA: Disgruntled Digital shareholders to hold meeting.
newsitem.headline: Disgruntled Digital shareholders to hold meeting.

text.p: A shareholder activist has organised a meeting of institutions that own Digital Equipment Corp. stock in New York next month to discuss the beleaguered company's poor performance.

Herbert Denton, who organised recent fights against the management of California Microwave Inc., Ashland Inc. and Comsat Computer Corp., expects owners of up to 40 percent of Digital's outstanding stock to attend the June 18 meeting.

"If Compaq thinks DEC is worth $60, and you look at the breakup value of DEC in the high $60s, you say hey, you know, the issues facing this company need to be understood by the institutional investment community," Denton said.

The Wall Street Journal reported this month that Compaq Computer Corp. reached a tentative agreement to buy Digital for $9 billion to $10 billion in 1995 but Digital backed away from the deal, which valued Digital at about $60 a share. Digital's shares have plunged since then.
Digital stock, which touched $25 earlier this year, rose 37.5 cents to $35.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
A spokesman for the Maynard, Mass.-based computer company said Chief Executive Robert Palmer and other executives did not plan on attending the shareholder meeting.
"We have an active investor relations programme and the company and the senior managers regularly communicate with shareholders and the investment community," Digital spokesman Dan Kaferle said.

Denton, president of the small New York broker-dealer Providence Capital Inc., holds a tiny amount of Digital stock, but believes his call for a meeting has touched a nerve in the investment community.

"Mr. Palmer has been in the saddle now for five years or so, 57,000 people have lost their jobs, so there's been radical change and the level of profitability at this time is not that strong," Denton said.
Over the past seven fiscal years, Digital has lost more than $5.8 billion, and for the first six months of its current fiscal year, the company has lost $25 million.
Palmer announced the third restructuring under his tenure in early April and has halved the number of employees to about 55,000, but the company has yet to return to a sustainable pattern of growth.
Denton said the New York meeting will serve as an information session to discuss the challenges facing Digital. He declined to say if any of the institutional shareholders had an agenda to pursue.

"Normally, when we've gotten to a point like this, we've got a very good idea of what strategic changes the major shareholders would be interested in," he said. "In the case of Digital, there are a lot of major issues facing the company that are not so clear cut."
Seven panellists including mainframe computer designers, intellectual property rights experts and Wall Street analysts will address the meeting, Denton said.
